Baboon Killing Fields

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Why have 4000 baboons been slaughtered in the pine forests near Sabi in Mpumalanga?

Unique Selling Point:
Baboon Matters Trust’s Jeni Trenhowan and Kathy Kelly have been investigating why beneath the pine plantations in Sabi, Mpumalanga are the skeletal remains of thousands of baboons.
They first heard about the baboons being killed back in 2008, when resident reported it to their trust. Back then, only 200 had been killed by the owners of the pine plantations becauase they believe the baboons ruin the bark on the trees which they make products like ironing baords and paper. Baboon matter raised awareness and the killing stopped. But, towards the end of last year, and in January informants on the ground suspected something was amiss. Upon further investigation 3 plantations – York (who make domestic products), Kavanti Land (which is government owned), and Sappi (paper), have allegedly killed 4000 baboons. This accroding to the department of envrionment and forrestry departments records, and the company’s confirm this.

Summary:
The organization snuck onto the plantations, and with the help of an informant called “Pierre” managed to capture video evidence of the following:
1. A boma-like cage (see video) in which they capture the baboons with hundreds of bones scattered around the area.
2. A mass grave site where hundreds of skeletons were found

The trust has made a short video which includes a little of their evidence – it has around 400 views. But, they will give us exclusive access to their video footage of a newer second mass grave with 300 hundred skeletons – many of them babies (family troop), access to their informants and exlusive access to their new information – the permits which were issued (2 to SAPPI who said they weren’t invovled) show that they only had permits to capture the baboons with nets, not kill them. Therefore this was unlawfull and they did not have the required permits. Baboon Matters has already PAIA’d both departments for further information – which they expect this week. We would have all of this exclusively.

My proposal would be to go to SABI – a day in advance of a presenter arriving – try and gain access to the plantations and the bones. (Need to check legally if we are allowed on property – Jeni explained that it is open, but there are defintely signs we aren’t supposed to be on their land.) We would interview the baboon matters people, and their informants with a presenter. We would request interviews with both departments and then go to the forrests and ask to all 3 of the pine plantations as well. (So that’s 5 sets of right of replys)

flights to nelspruit - one "reccie day" trying to get undercover footage.
camera crew hopefully from there
presenter flights to there
rental car in nelspruit
getty footage of drone visuals in forrest
baboon footage

Press Release:


Baboon Killings
It’s alleged that, since 2008, over 4000 baboons have been killed to reduce the destruction of pine plantations in Mpumalanga. Businesses claim it’s necessary because baboons are causing millions of Rands worth of damage, while on the other hand, conservationists are calling for an immediate ban on the killing of baboons. Carte Blanche investigates.


Script:


Shots of forests leading into luzanne pulling back brush A never-ending forest of pine trees in the remote area of Sabie, Mpumalanga. It may seem tranquil but the forest floor is littered with hundreds of Chacma baboon bones.
Luzanne - PRIME CREW Animal Activist Luzanne: “All of a sudden you’ll feel movement, underneath your feet, and it feels like you’re rollerskating along things, and you bend down and you move the pine needles away and you realize that you’re walking on bodies.”
Pierre Pierre: “Everywhere you look you see bones on the forest floor, people definitely know about what is going on.”
Jenni intro Baboon Matters Trust founder Jenni Threthowan says last year panicked Sabie locals called her cape town based NGO.
Jenni Jenni: “Baboon matters got lots of calls from residents in Sabie, who were saying, there’s these mass traps going up and we’re really worried.”
Pierre Sabie local Pierre Van der Walt was told about the bones by a timber plantation worker. He felt empathy for the creatures.
Pierre Pierre: “The have beautiful lively brown eyes, and they’re intelligent.”
Baboon licks camera lens
Baboon picking plant
Bark

Drone visual of forest These intelligent primates are known for their playful and mischievous nature. But to some, baboons are pests and are often shot by farmers for stealing their fruit and stripping the bark from trees. This is a serious economic problem for pine plantations.
Link – about plantations LINK: “There are 1.4 million hectres of pine forests in south Africa, now these trees can only be harvested, 25-30 years after they’ve been hand planted, they end up being used as furniture, or paper, or domestic products in your home.”
Mike Peters Mike: “Where there is damage upto 28% of plantations can be affected and the damage in those areas can be upto 50% of the trees completely killed.”
Michael Peters intro
Forestry South Africa’s Michael Peters represents the pine plantation industry, which employs 53-thousand people and adds 6 billion rand to the Mpumalanga GDP per annum.
Mike Peters Mike: “It gets to a point when you reach those levels of mortality that it’s no longer economically viable to try and harvest the timber.”
Link – no one knows why LINK: “Some speculate that it is to get to the sweet sap or insects or to use the bark for medicinal purposes, and some say it is to relieve stress, but no one really knows why the baboons strip the bark from the pine trees.”
Prof Les Brown intro – book + study Professor Leslie Brown is head of UNISA’s applied behavioural ecology and ecosystem research unit. He conducted one of the first studies on baboon bark stripping. The team included leading primatologists and was commissioned by the plantations in 2004.
Show visuals of baboons stripping Brown “They strip them from the tip of the growing point… the basic cambium of the plants is then exposed to the environment and then the plant will die and then they will chew that specific bark and they will spit out little balls which we found underneath.”
Show visuals of the trees dead Removing the bark around the entire circumference of a woody plant is called ring barking, and results in the death of the tree.
mike Mike: “it’s the whole value add of sawn timber products…You have literally millions of rands worth of damage on timber crops.”
Siya intro Deputy Director of the Forestry Regulation Unit within the Mpumalanga Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries Siyabulela Kobese says research is a top priority.
Siya: Siya: “There are a number of solutions that have been tried and tested, amongst the options, is the option of culling, and another option is that of capture and relocation.”
culling Culling reduces the wild animal population by shooting a selected family unit.
Link LINK: Chacma baboons are very family orientated, and just like us they grieve their lost ones.
Why they cull. Therefore, ethically, an entire troop of baboons – including the babies - must be selected and shot humanely.
siya Siya: “The view is that culling is the most ethical way of controlling the baboon population, but what is important about culling is that there is accountability and we are able to report on population levels.”
Culling numbers This need for transparency on numbers to stakeholders like the plantations and the NGO’s lead to the creation of the Baboon Damage Interest group which is chaired by environmental scientist John Scotcher.
scotcher John: “The current research seems to indicate that it’s largely stress related. But there is a theory that there possibly could be a sweetener in the trees which are attracting the baboons.”
Professor Brown says his team’s paper gave correct management strategies on how to solve the baboon damage enigma.
Brown - ecologist Brown: “We recommended that a proper scientific counting method should be used on how many baboon troops there were, and how many baboons were in those troops.”
Mike – forest SA Mike: “Typically with wild life one doesn’t do a census because the numbers are very high, and the areas are very large, so people do survey’s.
Culled numbers John was commissioned by Forest SA to further Brown’s research. John says 4000 baboons have been culled, that’s about 500 per year since 2008.
mike Mike: “Where they reduce their populations from the 7 to 8 baboons per sq km that we’re finding in plantations, down to 2 baboons per sq km, the stress levels drop and the damage ceases.”
“damage causing animals” But no one knows the actual baboon population numbers. Mike says no culling permit is necessary as baboons are labelled “damage causing animals.”
mike Mike: “There’s absolutely no risk of causing local extinctions and that’s certainly not our intention.”
Footage of baboons Nevertheless, culling is the chosen form of control. (pause)
We found these trap cages on the forest floor near Sabie. Animal activist Luzanne Kratz rehabilitates baboons who have been injured by cars, or shot by farmers for her NGO Prime Crew.
luzanne Luzanne: ““They bate the cages with mielies. We’ve realized that they’re ringing a bell everytime that they bate the cages, so they are actually enticing the baboons into this death trap.”
Culling? John advises the industry on the way ethical culling should be executed.
scotcher Scotcher: “The enclosure is quite large, it’s about 3m by 22m long and it’s got a door at either end, you identify the damage causing baboons, you get the entire troop is coming to that food, then you can release the two doors. Then the baboons are culled using a silencer and there is a process that you go through, which animals you shoot first.”
Buckshot shell casing – cage 1 footage Mark middleton from But, near the cages we found buckshot shell casings. Buckshot are lead pellets that spread out upon impact.
Vet Mark: “The buckshot is there to maime. We’re thinking they use that to incapacitate the baboons and then use the shotgun to finish them off.”
vet Veterinary scientist Dr. Mark Middleton has seen photos of the remains.
Vet SHORTEN Mark: “As it leaves the gun, it basically starts spreading so you’re getting this peppered effect on the body… you’re going to getting bleeding, pain, if you’re lucky you’ll kill that animal.”
Forestry SA Mike: “They’re not supposed to be using buckshot to shoot baboons.”
Claire: “Whose responsibility is it the monitor the culling process because it just feels like there seems to be no checks and balances in how the culling process is done?”
Mike: “I believe that is absolutely our responsibility, there are new regulations that we published last year to deal with damage causing animals that actually place that onus on the landowners, now we have done that voluntarily as the industry.”
Holdings skulls with claire Jenni recalls what several locals told her about the culling.
Jenni Jenni: “He said the screaming is awful, and he said the baboons shriek and when they’re in pain they shriek, it must be awful…”
Luzanne Luzanne: “The cages are double wired, so it strengthens the cage, they then hurl themselves against the wire, they are actually indenting the wire, they panic, it must be terrible.”
siya Siya: “I dont think anyone takes comfort in merely culling the baboons. If new practices or ways come up of trying to deal with the challenge, then those options will have to be explored.”
MIKE Mike: “The way the industry is dealing with it, is the most scientifically defensible and effective method.”
DAFF Siya: “When it comes to dealing then with the disposal of the corpses of the baboons, that should also be done in a manner that is dignified.”
Scotcher Scotcher: “Baboon carcasses, are disposed of in a deep pit. Bodies are disposed of by laying them two deep and then you put in about two and a half kilograms dolomitic lime per animal.”
Jenni Baboon matters lobbied the baboon damage interest group for a temporary stay or a moratorium, on the killings while more research was gathered.
Jenni Jenni: “I felt the number of baboons being killed was just escalating and they weren’t actually doing anything to find other solutions.”
moratorium The moratorium was not granted, and baboon matters left the interest group.
siya Siya: “It was not the correct platform for getting that moratorium issues. They should review their decision not to participate, because their voice is still needed in that forum.”
Jenni Jenni: “We have requested a meeting with the minister Molewa to ask her to impose a moratorium.”
UCT research A 5 year research study examined 49 different methods of controlling baboons. Funded by Forestry SA at UCT’s baboon research unit, the studies preliminary findings may answer why baboons strip the bark.
Siya Siya: “We will still continue to wait for the final research to be concluded, and also the peer review process, and then we will continue to engage, because the process is not going to be finalized by merely publishing the research.”
Mike Mike: “We end up humanizing this issue, and it’s understandable they’re primates. The final analysis: they are wild animals, their population levels are now at a stage where they are excessively stressed, and that is causing an impact on agriculture and forestry and that needs to be managed.”
ending For the plantation baboons, the balance between curbing the damage they create, and solutions for their longevity, is to put it mildly, a delicate one.

They should review their decision not to participate, because their voice is still needed in that forum.” Jenni Jenni: “We have requested a meeting with the minister Molewa to ask her to impose a moratorium.” UCT research A 5 year research study examined 49 different methods of controlling baboons. Funded by Forestry SA at UCT’s baboon research unit, the studies preliminary findings may answer why baboons strip the bark. Siya Siya: “We will still continue to wait for the final research to be concluded, and also the peer review process, and then we will continue to engage, because the process is not going to be finalized by merely publishing the research.” Mike Mike: “We end up humanizing this issue, and it’s understandable they’re primates. The final analysis: they are wild animals, their population levels are now at a stage where they are excessively stressed, and that is causing an impact on agriculture and forestry and that needs to be managed.” ending For the plantation baboons, the balance between curbing the damage they create, and solutions for their longevity, is to put it mildly, a delicate one. 11:08 PROMO 1: 10 SECONDER: Since 2008, 4000 Chacma baboons have been culled to reduce destruction to pine tree plantations in Mpumalanga. Carte Blanche investigates. PROMO 2: 15 SECONDER: Since 2008, over 4000 baboons have been killed to reduce damage to pine trees in Mpumalanga. We find out why. Mike: “The way the industry is dealing with it, is the most scientifically defensible and effective method.” PROMO 3: 15 SECONDER: Pierre: “Everywhere that you look you see bones on the forest floor.” Why have 4000 baboons been culled in the pine forests near Sabie in Mpumalanga? Mike: “it’s the whole value add of sawn timber products…You have literally millions of rands worth of damage.”

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Why have 4000 baboons been slaughtered in the pine forests near Sabi in Mpumalanga?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Baboon Matters Trust’s Jeni Trenhowan and Kathy Kelly have been investigating why beneath the pine plantations in Sabi, Mpumalanga are the skeletal remains of thousands of baboons. They first heard about the baboons being killed back in 2008, when resident reported it to their trust. Back then, only 200 had been killed by the owners of the pine plantations becauase they believe the baboons ruin the bark on the trees which they make products like ironing baords and paper. Baboon matter raised awareness and the killing stopped. But, towards the end of last year, and in January informants on the ground suspected something was amiss. Upon further investigation 3 plantations – York (who make domestic products), Kavanti Land (which is government owned), and Sappi (paper), have allegedly killed 4000 baboons. This accroding to the department of envrionment and forrestry departments records, and the company’s confirm this.
metadata.Summary: The organization snuck onto the plantations, and with the help of an informant called “Pierre” managed to capture video evidence of the following: 1. A boma-like cage (see video) in which they capture the baboons with hundreds of bones scattered around the area. 2. A mass grave site where hundreds of skeletons were found The trust has made a short video which includes a little of their evidence – it has around 400 views. But, they will give us exclusive access to their video footage of a newer second mass grave with 300 hundred skeletons – many of them babies (family troop), access to their informants and exlusive access to their new information – the permits which were issued (2 to SAPPI who said they weren’t invovled) show that they only had permits to capture the baboons with nets, not kill them. Therefore this was unlawfull and they did not have the required permits. Baboon Matters has already PAIA’d both departments for further information – which they expect this week. We would have all of this exclusively. My proposal would be to go to SABI – a day in advance of a presenter arriving – try and gain access to the plantations and the bones. (Need to check legally if we are allowed on property – Jeni explained that it is open, but there are defintely signs we aren’t supposed to be on their land.) We would interview the baboon matters people, and their informants with a presenter. We would request interviews with both departments and then go to the forrests and ask to all 3 of the pine plantations as well. (So that’s 5 sets of right of replys)
